title: SK Hynix: "First 3D DRAM product aims for mass production starting from 100 layers, within 4~5 years"
author: B
text:
F

Fred Chen
Moderator

Reporter Lee Jun
Published 2026.11.25 17:44

SK Hynix expects 3D DRAM to be commercialized around 2031. The first product is expected to be a memory cell stacked in 100 layers.

Choi Kang-sik, SK Hynix's DE (Distinguished Engineer), said on the 25th at the Seoul National University AI Semiconductor Forum held at Seoul National University in Gwanak-gu, Seoul, "We are developing 3D DRAM with the goal of mass production within the next 4~5 years."

Choi DE said, "To achieve an integration level similar to the current 10nm-class DRAM, about 75 layers of cells must be stacked," adding, "Considering additional factors, the first product will start with 100 layers."

Choi DE said that the first product's level of floors can be implemented with current equipment, but floors 200~300 and above require dedicated equipment development. In the long term, they also considered expanding layers beyond 1,000 layers using multi-stack and hybrid bonding technologies used in 3D NAND flash.

He also revealed that SK Hynix fabricated 3D DRAM cells to verify their operating characteristics. They explained that the refresh characteristic of periodically recharging the charge was also implemented at a level similar to that of existing DRAM.

3D DRAM is a structure where memory cells are stacked vertically. It is a different technology from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), which stacks multiple DRAM chips, or 3D stacked DRAM, which places DRAM on top of logic chips.

The reason for converting DRAM to a 3D structure is that miniaturization has reached its limit. DRAM stores charge in capacitors. As the cell area shrinks, the amount of charge that can be stored decreases, and leakage current and resistance increase. Instead of reducing cells, 3D DRAM can be stacked upward, solving charge issues and increasing integration.

3D DRAM is made by layering and etching silicon and silicon germanium (SiGe) in multiple layers. As the number of layers increases, the circuit connection structure becomes more complex and the etching difficulty rises.

SK Hynix proposed a 'selector' structure that selects only the necessary circuits and operates them as a solution. In this case, he explains that the area required for connection and the electrical load can be reduced. They are considering reducing costs by integrating etching process technology used in 3D NAND.

They are also researching ways to switch transistor channel materials from silicon to indium gallium zinc oxide (IGZO). IGZO has less leakage current than silicon, which can extend data retention time. However, the challenge is to resolve the changes in properties caused by hydrogen and other factors.

Choi DE said, "If IGZO's reliability is ensured, it could be a game changer in 3D DRAM."
